body:
A Tentative List is not the World Heritage List

India maintains a Tentative List of sites that it may consider for future World Heritage nominations. These places may possess substantial historical or architectural importance, but their appearance on the Tentative List does not mean UNESCO has inscribed them as World Heritage properties.

This distinction is especially important for Gujarat because some famous historical sites appear on the Tentative List while others are already inscribed.

Sun Temple, Modhera

The Sun Temple at Modhera is located in Mehsana district. It is an important example of western Indian Maru-Gurjara temple architecture, associated with the Solanki dynasty and the reign of Bhimdev I in the 11th century. NCERT dates its construction to 1026.

The temple complex is especially recognised for its sculptural decoration, its assembly hall and its stepped water tank known as the Surya Kund. The relationship between the east-facing temple and the sun is also an important architectural feature.

UNESCO status: Sun Temple, Modhera and its adjoining monuments was submitted to India's Tentative List on 13 December 2022. As of 23 November 2026, it is not an inscribed World Heritage property.

Modhera and Konark must not be confused

Both Modhera and Konark are associated with sun temples, but only Sun Temple, Konark, in Odisha, is on the World Heritage List. Konark was inscribed in 1984. Modhera is in Gujarat and remains a Tentative List entry at the stated cutoff.

Harappan port-town of Lothal

Lothal is a Harappan archaeological site in Dholka taluka of Ahmedabad district. It is associated with planned settlement, craft production and maritime trade. Its archaeological remains include structures interpreted as a warehouse and a large basin commonly identified as a dockyard.

UNESCO status: Archaeological remains of a Harappa Port-Town, Lothal was submitted to India's Tentative List on 15 April 2014. It is not an inscribed World Heritage property as of 23 November 2026.

In contrast, Dholavira is an inscribed Harappan World Heritage property, recognised in 2021. Both sites belong to the Harappan cultural sphere, but they are distinct archaeological locations with different UNESCO statuses.

Compare Gujarat's inscribed and tentative properties

A site's importance and its UNESCO status answer different questions. Its archaeological remains or architecture explain why it matters; the official UNESCO record establishes whether it is actually inscribed.

A site may also be protected under Indian heritage law without being on the UNESCO World Heritage List. National legal protection and international inscription must therefore be identified separately.

Prelims focus

  • Modhera Sun Temple: Mehsana district, Solanki period, 11th century.
  • Modhera Tentative List submission: 2022.
  • Lothal: Harappan port-town, Ahmedabad district.
  • Lothal Tentative List submission: 2014.
  • Konark Sun Temple: Odisha, World Heritage inscription in 1984.
  • Trap: The 2014 date for Lothal is its tentative submission, not a World Heritage inscription.

[UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Tentative List entry 6627, Sun Temple, Modhera and its adjoining monuments, submission dated 13 December 2022; Tentative List entry 5918, Archaeological remains of a Harappa Port-Town, Lothal, submission dated 15 April 2014; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, India State Party profile and Sun Temple, Konark, property 246; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class XI, chapter Temple Architecture and Sculpture, printed pp. 75–76. UNESCO records consulted 23 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Gujarat's four inscribed World Heritage properties and two Tentative List entries have distinct statuses; historical importance alone does not establish inscription.
pictures.caption: Inscribed World Heritage properties and Tentative List entries belong to different status categories.

title: Gujarat Heritage on the Tentative List and Commonly Confused Sites

body:
Matching Indian World Heritage properties with states

World Heritage questions often require a candidate to connect a recognised property with its state or union territory, its broad historical identity and sometimes its UNESCO inscription year. A property can contain several monuments or even multiple geographically separate components.

The following selection covers prominent cultural properties and recent inscriptions. The years are UNESCO inscription years, not construction dates. The status is based on UNESCO's World Heritage List as of 23 November 2026.

Cultural World Heritage propertyState or union territoryInscription year

Ellora CavesMaharashtra1983
Taj MahalUttar Pradesh1983

Archaeological Site of Nalanda MahaviharaBihar2016
Jaipur CityRajasthan2019
Kakatiya Rudreshwara (Ramappa) TempleTelangana2021
Sacred Ensembles of the HoysalasKarnataka2023

Ancient Buddhist Site of SarnathUttar Pradesh2026

Recent additions and their identities

Moidams: Ahom burial heritage

The Moidams at Charaideo in Assam are mound-burial structures associated with the Ahom dynasty. They were inscribed in 2024. Their identification depends on the connection between Ahom rulers, burial mounds and Assam.

Maratha Military Landscapes: a property across 2 states

The Maratha Military Landscapes of India was inscribed in 2025. It is a serial property consisting of 12 fortifications. Of these, 11 are in Maharashtra and 1, Gingee Fort, is in Tamil Nadu.

A serial World Heritage property contains multiple components recognised together because they express a connected heritage value. Thus, counting the 12 forts as 12 separate World Heritage properties would be incorrect.

Ancient Buddhist Site of Sarnath

Sarnath, in Uttar Pradesh, was inscribed in 2026. It is associated with the Buddhist tradition that identifies it as the place where the Buddha delivered his first sermon. The inscribed serial property preserves important archaeological and architectural remains, including stupas and monastic remains.

Natural and mixed World Heritage properties

Although the present subject emphasises architecture and built heritage, objective questions may test whether a recognised place is cultural, natural or mixed.

PropertyLocationCategoryInscription year
Kaziranga National ParkAssamNatural1985
Keoladeo National ParkRajasthanNatural1985
Sundarbans National ParkWest BengalNatural1987
Western GhatsMaharashtra, Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil NaduNatural2012
Khangchendzonga National ParkSikkimMixed2016

Khangchendzonga National Park is India's only mixed World Heritage property at the stated cutoff. Its mixed classification reflects both natural significance and cultural associations. It should not be placed in the exclusively natural category.

Prelims focus

  • Bhimbetka: Madhya Pradesh, prehistoric rock shelters, 2003.
  • Hampi: Karnataka, 1986; Khajuraho: Madhya Pradesh, 1986.
  • Konark: Odisha, 1984; Mahabalipuram: Tamil Nadu, 1984.
  • Moidams: Assam, 2024.
  • Maratha Military Landscapes: 2025, 12 forts in Maharashtra and Tamil Nadu.
  • Trap: Khangchendzonga National Park is mixed, not exclusively natural.

[UNESCO World Heritage Centre, India State Party profile, complete inscribed-property list and category classification; Maratha Military Landscapes of India, property 1739; Moidams – the Mound-Burial System of the Ahom Dynasty, property 1711; Ancient Buddhist Site of Sarnath, property 927; Khangchendzonga National Park, property 1513; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class XI, chapter Prehistoric Rock Paintings, printed pp. 3–5. UNESCO records consulted 23 November 2026.]

title: Important World Heritage Properties Across India: States, Years and Categories

body:
The five domains of intangible cultural heritage

The 2003 UNESCO Convention identifies 5 broad domains through which intangible cultural heritage may be expressed. These domains help classify living heritage, but they are not mutually exclusive. A single festival may involve music, oral tradition, ritual and craftsmanship.

  • Oral traditions and expressions: Spoken and recited cultural knowledge, including traditions transmitted through language.
  • Performing arts: Traditional dance, music, theatre and related expressions.
  • Social practices, rituals and festive events: Community celebrations, observances and customary practices.
  • Knowledge and practices concerning nature and the universe: Traditional knowledge and practices connected with people's understanding of the world.
  • Traditional craftsmanship: Knowledge and skills involved in making traditional objects.

For example, Vedic chanting illustrates an oral tradition; Chhau is a performing art; Garba combines performing arts with ritual and festive practice; and the Thatheras' metalworking tradition illustrates traditional craftsmanship.

India's 16 inscribed elements

According to UNESCO's India intangible cultural heritage profile, 16 elements were inscribed on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity as of 23 November 2026. The table gives their UNESCO inscription years and principal regional associations.

Inscription yearIntangible heritage elementPrincipal regional association
2008Kutiyattam, Sanskrit theatreKerala
2008Tradition of Vedic chantingAcross India
2008Ramlila, the traditional performance of the RamayanaPredominantly North India
2009Ramman, religious festival and ritual theatre of the Garhwal HimalayasUttarakhand
2010Chhau danceOdisha, Jharkhand and West Bengal
2010Kalbelia folk songs and dancesRajasthan
2010Mudiyettu, ritual theatre and dance dramaKerala
2012Buddhist chanting of LadakhLadakh
2013Sankirtana, ritual singing, drumming and dancingManipur
2014Traditional brass and copper utensil-making among the Thatheras of Jandiala GuruPunjab
2016YogaAcross India
2017Kumbh MelaPrayagraj, Haridwar, Ujjain and Nashik
2021Durga Puja in KolkataWest Bengal
2023Garba of GujaratGujarat
2024Nawrouz and its regional name variantsMultinational element including India
2025DeepavaliAcross India

Important distinctions within the list

Several traditions belong to more than one state

Chhau is associated with Odisha, Jharkhand and West Bengal. It is therefore incorrect to treat it as a tradition belonging exclusively to one state. Kumbh Mela is likewise associated with several pilgrimage centres rather than a single location.

Traditional craftsmanship means the skill, not only the object

The 2014 Thatheras inscription concerns traditional brass and copper utensil-making practices at Jandiala Guru in Punjab. It is not an inscription of a particular brass vessel as a World Heritage monument. This is a useful example of how a material object can be associated with an intangible cultural practice.

A single inscription may involve more than one country

Nawrouz, also written in several related forms such as Nowruz and Navruz, is a multinational intangible heritage element. UNESCO's India listing records it under 2024. Its recognition should not be understood as an exclusively Indian tradition.

Different traditions may share a region

Kutiyattam and Mudiyettu are both associated with Kerala, but they are different traditions and appear as distinct UNESCO elements. Similarly, the association of Kalbelia with Rajasthan must not be confused with the association of Garba with Gujarat.

For the 3 entries recorded in 2008, UNESCO's present Representative List year is 2008. These traditions had earlier been recognised through UNESCO's former Masterpieces programme. In a question asking for the year shown on the present Representative List, use 2008.

Prelims focus

  • 2008: Kutiyattam, Vedic chanting and Ramlila.
  • 2010: Chhau, Kalbelia and Mudiyettu.
  • 2014: Thatheras' traditional brass and copper craft, Punjab.
  • 2021: Durga Puja in Kolkata; 2023: Garba of Gujarat.
  • 2024: Nawrouz, multinational; 2025: Deepavali.
  • Trap: The 16 entries are intangible heritage elements, not 16 World Heritage properties.

[UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, India, Elements on the Lists and Representative List entries, status checked 23 November 2026; UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, Intangible Heritage Domains in the 2003 Convention, Article 2; UNESCO, India to Host the 20th Session of the Committee in 2025, published 31 January 2025, historical list of 15 entries before Deepavali's inscription.]

pictures.alt: The 5 living-heritage domains with Indian examples; Garba of Gujarat overlaps performing arts with social, ritual and festive practices.
pictures.caption: The 2003 Convention recognises 5 broad, sometimes overlapping domains of living heritage.

title: India's UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage Elements and Their Regions
